newsitem.title: CHILE: Gephardt says Chile should not seek entry to NAFTA.
newsitem.headline: Gephardt says Chile should not seek entry to NAFTA.

text.p: Chile should negotiate a separate bilateral trade deal with the United States rather than seek entry in the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), U.S. House of Representatives minority leader Richard Gephardt said Thursday.

Because each country is unique, and because I believe we should improve on NAFTA, I would hope that we could reach a bilateral agreement between the United States and Chile," the Missouri Democrat told a news conference. NAFTA's original partners, Canada, Mexico and the United States, invited Chile in 1994 to open negotiations to join their pact.
But those talks stalled in 1995 because the United States failed to renew so-called fast track authority that would allow the White House to negotiate and sign new trade treaties.

Gephardt, an outspoken critic of NAFTA, added that a U.S.- Chile agreement should include provisions on labor and environmental protection with mutually agreed trade sanctions to ensure their enforcement. President Bill Clinton is due to send a proposal on fast track to the U.S. Congress around September 8. According to Gephardt, legislators would act on that bill late next month or early in October.

"It is hard to know now exactly what will be the fate of the fast track suggestion. I'm urging the U.S. administration to do this in a certain way. That decision has not been made yet, so it's hard for me to give you a projection on whether or not it will be approved," he said.

Fast track authorizations have traditionally given U.S. presidents a free hand to negotiate with any country or international trade body, but Gephardt said he hoped the upcoming bill would apply only to Chile.

"I want to try to do that because I believe that it would be very useful to have a bilateral treaty with Chile that could serve as a model for further trade negotiations with other countries, not only in Latin America but across the world," he added.
Gephardt declined to say whether he would support any fast track proposal Clinton, a fellow Democrat, might make next month, or only a request tailored to his tastes.
"Obviously I have to see what is proposed and I will make that evaluation at that time," he said.
Recalling the fast track bill he supported in 1991 for Republican president George Bush, the Democratic leader said he now wanted to see more specific language on labor and environmental protection.
Gephardt was in Santiago for a two-day stop on a South American tour that includes Venezuela, Brazil and Argentina. On Wednesday he met Chilean President Eduardo Frei.
